name: How do you coordinate specialty finishes and custom millwork with the architectural set?

mainEntity.name: How should custom cabinetry, stone, built-ins, and specialty finishes be coordinated so the architectural drawings stay accurate?
mainEntity.text: How should custom cabinetry, stone, built-ins, and specialty finishes be coordinated so the architectural drawings stay accurate?

acceptedAnswer.text: Custom millwork, stone, and specialty finishes need tighter coordination than standard construction items because they often depend on exact dimensions and sequencing. The architectural set should show the intended locations, sizes, and clearances, while shop drawings and finish schedules confirm how the items will actually be built. That includes backing, reveals, material thicknesses, appliance clearances, lighting placement, and adjacent wall or floor conditions. The biggest risk is designing beautiful custom elements that do not fit once framing, drywall, waterproofing, or tile buildup is added. That is why the coordination review should happen before fabrication, not after. The team should compare millwork drawings, cabinet shop drawings, stone templates, and finish plans against the latest architectural set. For high-end homes, this also affects visual alignment. A range hood, niche, panel seam, or fireplace surround may need small adjustments to maintain symmetry. Ask whether the coordinator reviews shop drawings against the architectural intent and whether field measurements are required before final fabrication. That step often prevents expensive remakes.
acceptedAnswer.description: Specialty finishes should be coordinated through detailed dimensions, shop drawings, and finish schedules that match the architectural plans. The architect and coordinator should verify clearances, reveals, backing, material thicknesses, and installation tolerances before fabrication. Otherwise, custom items may not fit the built space correctly.
